e-3722.knowledge_point: Determining Intervals on Which the Derivative of a Graphed Function Is Positive or Negative
e-3722.problem:
The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown below. The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=1$ and $x=4.$ Given that $f'(x) = 0$ at both $A$ and $B,$ find the intervals where $f'(x)>0.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14014428/assets/1a8208a75b7df62a0c692e08f74509ecf1462e3ab1f8dd7eae85a56272abde48.png)
e-3722.worked_solution:
We have $f'(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then $f'(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then $f'(x)<0.$

The information about $f'(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,1) & 1 & (1,4) & 4 & (4,+\infty ) \\ f & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ \\ {f}^{′} & - & 0 & + & 0 & -\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f'(x)>0$ on the interval $(1,4).$

decision.explanation: The curve rises for x < -3 and x > 3, so f'(x) > 0 on those intervals. It falls between -3 and 3, with a horizontal tangent at x = 0.

after.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,-3) & -3 & (-3,0) & 0 & (0,3) & 3 & (3,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{no extr.} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the intervals $(-\infty ,-3)$ and $(3,\infty ).$

Question 1
?

The graph of the continuous function y=f(x) is shown above. The points A,B, and C lie on the curve and have x-coordinates x=−3, x=0, and x=3. Given that f′(x)=0 at A,B, and C, find the intervals where f′(x)>0.

a
(−∞,−3) and (−3,0) and (3,∞)
b
(−∞,−3) and (3,∞)
c
(−∞,−3) and (0,∞)
d
(−∞,0) and (3,∞)
e
(−∞,−3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We have f′(x)=0 at the critical points A and B. Note the following:

  • If f(x) is strictly increasing, then f′(x)>0.

  • If f(x) is strictly decreasing, then f′(x)<0.

The information about f′(x) can be summarized in the following table:

x(−∞,−3)−3(−3,0)0(0,3)3(3,∞)f↗max↘no extr.↘min↗f′+0−0−0+

Therefore, f′(x)>0 on the intervals (−∞,−3) and (3,∞).

The graph of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ is shown above. The points $A,B,$ and $C$ lie on the curve and have $x$-coordinates $x=-3,$ $x=0,$ and $x=3.$ Given that ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $A,B,$ and $C,$ find the intervals where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$
content.worked_solution:
We have ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at the critical points $A$ and $B.$ Note the following:

- If $f(x)$ is strictly increasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- If $f(x)$ is strictly decreasing, then ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

The information about ${f}^{′}(x)$ can be summarized in the following table:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & (-\infty ,-3) & -3 & (-3,0) & 0 & (0,3) & 3 & (3,\infty ) \\ f & ↗ & \text{max} & ↘ & \text{no extr.} & ↘ & \text{min} & ↗ \\ {f}^{′} & + & 0 & - & 0 & - & 0 & +\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ on the intervals $(-\infty ,-3)$ and $(3,\infty ).$
